Book of Lemmas IX

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Two straight lines cross inside a circle at a right angle. Look at the four curved pieces of the circle between their ends.
How to play: Drag the horizontal or vertical line, or focus its handle and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claim to see whether the two sums stay the same.
Look for the math

Two chords cross at a right angle. The four arcs between their ends change size as you drag, but Archimedes found that two pairs of them always balance.

The exact claim

Name the ends so that A is left, B is right, C is below and D is above. The proposition says

arc AD + arc CB = arc AC + arc DB

The article below adds something stronger: each sum is a semicircle, 180° or π radians. Drag the chords and watch the two numbers in the status line stay at 180°, even when one chord passes through the centre.

Why a half turn?

The angle where two chords meet is half the sum of the arcs it cuts off. At the crossing O the angle AOD opens towards the arcs AD and CB, so

arc AD + arc CB = 2∠AOD

Because the chords are perpendicular, ∠AOD = 90°, and the sum is a half turn. The other angle at O opens towards AC and DB and is also 90°, giving arc AC + arc DB = 180°. This is the intersecting chords theorem in its angular form. The logic test checks all of this on thousands of configurations, including chords that pass through the centre; the article excludes those in its wording, but the equality still holds.

About this picture

The article cited below is prose with a still drawing; it does not embed the applet. The moving picture here follows Bogomolny's BOL9 applet: the circle keeps its size, the chords stay horizontal and vertical, and each coloured arc uses the applet's own start angle and signed sweep. One harmless quirk of that applet is kept: because it measures angles from the rightmost point of the circle, its coloured strokes sit a half turn away from the endpoints they name. Their lengths, and therefore the sums, are exactly the same. The applet's drag stops when the crossing comes within 5 pixels of the circle; this page keeps that same limit.

Try sliding one chord almost to the edge of the circle: each sum still closes at 180°.
